question.text: The general solution of the differential equation $\frac{d x}{d t}=\frac{x \log x}{t}$ is

solution.text: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{d x}{d t}=\frac{x \log x}{t} \\ & \therefore \int \frac{d x}{x \log x}=\int \frac{d t}{t} \\ & \therefore \log |\log x|=\log |t|+\log c \\ & \therefore \log x=t c \Rightarrow x=e^{t c}\end{aligned}$

question.text: The general solution of the differential equation $\frac{d y}{d x}=2^{y-x}$ is

solution.text: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{d y}{d x}=2^{y-x} \\ & \therefore \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{2^y}{2^x} \Rightarrow \int \frac{d y}{2^y}=\int \frac{d x}{2^x} \\ & \therefore \int 2^{-y} d y=\int 2^{-x} d x \Rightarrow \frac{2^{-y}}{-\ell n 2}=\frac{2^{-x}}{-\ln 2}+c_1 \Rightarrow \frac{2^{-y}}{\ln 2}=\frac{2^{-x}}{\ln 2}-c_1 \\ & \therefore \frac{1}{\ln 2}\left[2^{-x}-2^{-y}\right]=c_1 \\ & \therefore \frac{1}{2^x}-\frac{1}{2^y}=c, \text { where } c=\left(c_1\right)(\ln 2)\end{aligned}$

question.text: The general solution of the differential equation $(2 y-1) d x-(2 x+3) d y=0$ is

solution.text: $\begin{aligned} & (2 y-1) d x-(2 x+3) d y=0 \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{(2 y-1)}{(2 x+3)} \\ & \therefore \int \frac{d y}{2 y-1}=\int \frac{d x}{2 x+3} \\ & \frac{\log |2 y-1|}{2}=\frac{\log |2 x+3|}{2}+\log c_1 \Rightarrow \log \left|\frac{2 x+3}{2 y-1}\right|=-\log c_1=\log c \\ & \therefore \frac{2 x+3}{2 y-1}=c\end{aligned}$

question.text: The particular solution of the differential equation $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{y+1}{x^2-x}$, when $\mathrm{x}=2$ and $\mathrm{y}=1$ is

solution.text: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{y+1}{x^2-x} \\ & \therefore \int \frac{d y}{y+1}=\int \frac{d x}{x(x-1)} \\ & \therefore \int \frac{d y}{y+1}=\int\left[\frac{1}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x}\right] d x \Rightarrow \log |y+1|=\log |x-1|-\log |x|+ \\ & \log c \\ & \text { We have } x=2 \text { and } y=1 \\ & \therefore \log |2|=\log |1|-\log |1|+\log c \Rightarrow c=2 \\ & \therefore \log |y+1|=\log |x-1|-\log |x|+\log |2| \\ & \log |y+1|=\log \left|\frac{2(x-1)}{x}\right| \\ & \therefore y+1=\frac{2(x-1)}{x} \Rightarrow x y+x=2 x-2 \Rightarrow x y=x-2\end{aligned}$

question.text: The general solution of $\sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)=x+y$ is

solution.text: $\begin{aligned} & \sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)=x+y \\ & \therefore \frac{d y}{d x}=\sin (x+y) \\ & \text { Put } x+y=t \quad \Rightarrow 1+\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d t}{d x} \\ & \therefore \frac{d t}{d x}-1=\sin t \Rightarrow \frac{d t}{d x}=1+\sin t \\ & \therefore \int \frac{d t}{1+\sin t}=\int d x \\ & \therefore \int \frac{(1-\sin t) d t}{1-\sin } t=\int d x \Rightarrow \int \frac{1-\sin t}{\cos ^2 t} d t=\int d x \\ & \Rightarrow \int\left(\sec ^2 t-\operatorname{sect} \tan t\right) d t=\int d x \\ & \therefore \tan t-\sec t=x+c \\ & \therefore \tan (x+y)-\sec (x+y)=x+c\end{aligned}$

question.text: The particular solution of the differential equation $y(1+\log x)=\left(\log x^x\right) \frac{d y}{d x}$, when $y(e)=e^2$ is

solution.text:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& y(1+\log x)=\left(\log x^x\right) \frac{d y}{d x} \\
& \therefore \int \frac{(1+\log x)}{\left(\log x^x\right)}=\int \frac{d y}{y}
\end{aligned}
$$
We know that $\frac{d}{d x}\left(\log x^x\right)=(1+\log x) d x$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \log \left|\log \mathrm{x}^{\mathrm{x}}\right|=\log |\mathrm{y}|+\log \mathrm{c} \\
& \text { We have } \mathrm{y}(\mathrm{e})=\mathrm{e}^2 \\
& \therefore \log \left|\log \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{e}}\right|=\log \left|\mathrm{e}^2\right|+\log \mathrm{c} \\
& \therefore \log |\mathrm{e} \log \mathrm{e}|=2 \log |\mathrm{e}|+\log \mathrm{c} \\
& \therefore 1=2+\log \mathrm{c} \Rightarrow \log \mathrm{c}=-1 \\
& \therefore \log \left|\log \mathrm{x}^{\mathrm{x}}\right|=\log |\mathrm{y}|-\log \mathrm{e} \\
& \therefore \log |\mathrm{x} \log \mathrm{x}|+\log \mathrm{e}=\log |\mathrm{y}| \\
& \therefore \mathrm{ex} \log \mathrm{x}-\mathrm{y}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

question.text:
The general solution of the differential equation.
$$
\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \cos \left(\frac{y}{x}\right) d x-\left[\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) \sin \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+\cos \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)\right] d y=0 \text { is }
$$

solution.text:
We have $\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \cos \left(\frac{y}{x}\right) d x-\left[\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) \sin \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+\cos \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)\right] d y=0$
$$
\therefore \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \cos \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}{\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) \sin \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+\cos \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}
$$
Put $\frac{y}{x}=v \Rightarrow y=v x \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=v+x \frac{d v}{d x}$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \mathrm{v}+\mathrm{x} \frac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{dx}}=\frac{\mathrm{v} \cos \mathrm{v}}{\frac{1}{\mathrm{v}} \sin \mathrm{v}+\cos \mathrm{v}}=\frac{\mathrm{v}^2 \cos \mathrm{v}}{\sin \mathrm{v}+\mathrm{v} \cos \mathrm{v}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{x} \frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{dx}}=\frac{-\mathrm{v} \sin \mathrm{v}}{\sin \mathrm{v}+\mathrm{v} \cos \mathrm{v}} \\
& \therefore \int \frac{\sin \mathrm{v}+\mathrm{v} \cos \mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{v} \sin \mathrm{v}} \mathrm{dv}=\int \frac{-\mathrm{dx}}{\mathrm{x}} \Rightarrow \int \frac{1}{\mathrm{v}} \mathrm{dv}+\int \cot \mathrm{v} d \mathrm{v}=-\int \frac{\mathrm{dx}}{\mathrm{x}} \\
& \therefore \log |\mathrm{v}|+\log |+\sin \mathrm{x}|=-\log |\mathrm{x}|+\log \mathrm{k} \Rightarrow \log |(\mathrm{v})(\sin \mathrm{v})(\mathrm{x})| \\
& =\log \mathrm{k}
\end{aligned}
$$
$\therefore y \sin \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)=k$

question.text:
The general solution of the differential equation
$$
y(1+\log x)\left(\frac{d x}{d y}\right)
$$
$-x \log x=0$ is

solution.text:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& y(1+\log x)\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)-x \log x=0 \\
& \therefore \int \frac{(1+\log x)}{x \log x} d x=\int \frac{d y}{y} \\
& \int \frac{d x}{x \log x}+\int \frac{d x}{x}=\int \frac{d y}{y} \\
& \therefore \log (\log x)+\log x=\log y+\log c \\
& \therefore \log [x \log x]=\log (y, c)
\Rightarrow x \log x=y c
\end{aligned}
$$

question.text: The general solution of the differential equation $x+y \frac{d y}{d x}=\sec \left(x^2+y^2\right)$ is

solution.text: $\begin{aligned} & \text { We have, } x+y \frac{d y}{d x}=\sec \left(x^2+y^2\right) \\ & \text { Put } x^2+y^2=u \Rightarrow 2 x+2 y \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d u}{d x} \\ & \therefore x+y \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{d u}{d x} \\ & \therefore \frac{1}{2} \frac{d u}{d x}=\sec u \\ & \therefore \int \frac{d u}{\sec u}=\int 2 d x \\ & \therefore \sin u=2 x+c \\ & \Rightarrow \sin \left(x^2+y^2\right)=2 x+c\end{aligned}$

question.text: A differential equation for the temperature ' $\mathrm{T}$ ' of a hot body as a function of time, when it is placed in a both which is held at a constant temperature of $32^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$, is given by (where $\mathrm{k}$ is a constant of proportionality)

solution.text:
The temperature $\mathrm{T}$ of the body will decrease with time. The body is kept in a bath of temperature $32^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$.
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \frac{\mathrm{dT}}{\mathrm{dt}} \alpha-(\mathrm{T}-32) \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{dT}}{\mathrm{dt}}=-\mathrm{k}(\mathrm{T}-32)

$$

question.text: The general solution of the differential equation $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{x+y+1}{x+y-1}$ is given by
The solution of the differential equation $\sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x}\right)=x+\mathrm{y}$ is

solution.text:
We have $\sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)=x+y$
$$
\therefore \frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{dx}}=\sin (\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{y})
$$
Put $\quad x+y=t \Rightarrow y=t-x \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d t}{d x}-1$
$$
\therefore \frac{\mathrm{dt}}{\mathrm{dx}}=1+\sin \mathrm{t} \Rightarrow \int \frac{\mathrm{dt}}{1+\sin \mathrm{t}}=\int \mathrm{dx}
$$
$\int \frac{(1-\sin t)}{(1+\sin t)(1-\sin t)} d t=\int d x \Rightarrow x=\int \frac{1-\sin t}{1-\sin ^{2} t} d t$

question.text: The general solution of the differential equation $\left(1+y^{2}\right)+\left(x-e^{\tan ^{-1} y}\right) \frac{d y}{d x}=0$ is

solution.text:
(A)
$\begin{array}{l}
\left(1+y^{2}\right)+\left(x-e^{\tan ^{-1} y}\right) \frac{d y}{d x}=0 \\
\therefore \quad\left(x-e^{\tan ^{-1} y}\right) \frac{d y}{d x}=-\left(1+y^{2}\right) \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{-\left(1+y^{2}\right)}{x-e^{\tan ^{-1} y}} \\
\therefore \frac{d x}{d y}=\frac{\left(x-e^{\tan ^{-1} y}\right)}{-\left(1+y^{2}\right)} \Rightarrow \frac{d x}{d y}=\frac{-x}{\left(1+y^{2}\right)}+\frac{e^{\tan ^{-1} y}}{1+y^{2}} \\
\therefore \frac{d x}{d y}+\frac{x}{1+y^{2}}=\frac{e^{\tan ^{-1} y}}{1+y^{2}} \\
\quad \text { I.F. }=e^{\int \frac{1}{1+y^{2}} d y}=e^{\tan ^{-1} y}
\end{array}$
So, the general solution is
$\begin{array}{l}
x \cdot e^{\tan ^{-1} y}=\int \frac{e^{\tan ^{-1} y}}{1+y^{2}} \cdot e^{\tan ^{-1} y} d x \\
\text { Put } e^{\tan ^{-1} y}=t \Rightarrow \frac{e^{\tan ^{-1} y}}{1+y^{2}} d y=d t \\
\therefore x \cdot e^{\tan ^{-1} y}=\int t d t \\
\therefore x \cdot e^{\tan ^{-1} y}=\frac{t^{2}}{2}+c \Rightarrow x \cdot e^{\tan ^{-1} y}=\frac{\left(e^{\tan ^{-1} y}\right)^{2}}{2}+c
\end{array}$

question.text: If $x\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y(\log y - \log x + 1)$ and its solution is $y = [h(x)]e^{cx}$, then $h(x) = \ldots$

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $x\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y(\log y - \log x + 1)$.

This can be rewritten as:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y}{x} \left( \log\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) + 1 \right)$

Let $y = vx$. Differentiating with respect to $x$, we get:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$

Substituting this into the differential equation:

$v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = v (\log v + 1)$

$v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = v \log v + v$

$x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = v \log v$

Separating the variables:

$\dfrac{dv}{v \log v} = \dfrac{dx}{x}$

Integrating both sides:

$\int \dfrac{dv}{v \log v} = \int \dfrac{dx}{x}$

$\log(\log v) = \log x + C$

$\log v = e^{\log x + C} = e^C x$

Let $e^C = c$, an arbitrary constant. Then:

$\log v = cx$

Substituting $v = \dfrac{y}{x}$:

$\log\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) = cx$

$\dfrac{y}{x} = e^{cx}$

$y = x e^{cx}$

Comparing this with the given solution $y = [h(x)]e^{cx}$, we get:

$h(x) = x$

Answer: $x$

question.text: The solution of the differential equation $x^2 y\,dx - (x^3 + y^3)\,dy = 0$ is

solution.text:
The given differential equation can be written as:

$\dfrac{dx}{dy} = \dfrac{x^3 + y^3}{x^2 y}$

This is a homogeneous differential equation. Substituting $x = vy$, we get:

$\dfrac{dx}{dy} = v + y\dfrac{dv}{dy}$

Substituting this into the differential equation:

$v + y\dfrac{dv}{dy} = \dfrac{v^3 y^3 + y^3}{v^2 y^3}$

$v + y\dfrac{dv}{dy} = \dfrac{v^3 + 1}{v^2}$

$v + y\dfrac{dv}{dy} = v + \dfrac{1}{v^2}$

$y\dfrac{dv}{dy} = \dfrac{1}{v^2}$

Separating the variables:

$v^2\,dv = \dfrac{dy}{y}$

Integrating both sides:

$\int v^2\,dv = \int \dfrac{dy}{y}$

$\dfrac{v^3}{3} = \log|y| - c$

Substituting $v = \dfrac{x}{y}$ back into the equation:

$\dfrac{x^3}{3y^3} = \log|y| - c$

$\log|y| - \dfrac{x^3}{3y^3} = c$

Answer: $\log|y| - \dfrac{x^3}{3y^3} = c$

question.text: If the general solution of the differential equation $y\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)dx - \left(x\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) - y\right)dy = 0$ is $\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) + g(y) = c$, then $g(y) = \ldots$

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $y\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)dx - \left(x\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) - y\right)dy = 0$

Rearranging the terms, we get:

$y\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)dx - x\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)dy + y dy = 0$

Dividing the entire equation by $y^2$, we obtain:

$\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)\left(\dfrac{y dx - x dy}{y^2}\right) + \dfrac{dy}{y} = 0$

Using the quotient rule for differentials, $d\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) = \dfrac{y dx - x dy}{y^2}$, the equation can be written as:

$\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)d\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) + \dfrac{dy}{y} = 0$

Integrating both sides, we get:

$\int \sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)d\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) + \int \dfrac{dy}{y} = c$

$\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) + \log|y| = c$

Comparing this with the given general solution $\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) + g(y) = c$, we find:

$g(y) = \log|y|$

Answer: $\log|y|$

question.text:
If the function $f(x)$ satisfying the equation $[f'(x)]^2 + 4f(x)f'(x) + f^2(x) = 0$, then $f(x) = $
(where $c$ is constant of integration)

solution.text:
Given the differential equation:

$[f'(x)]^2 + 4f(x)f'(x) + f^2(x) = 0$

This is a quadratic equation in $f'(x)$. Solving for $f'(x)$ using the quadratic formula:

$f'(x) = \dfrac{-4f(x) \pm \sqrt{16f^2(x) - 4(1)(f^2(x))}}{2}$

$f'(x) = \dfrac{-4f(x) \pm \sqrt{12f^2(x)}}{2}$

$f'(x) = \dfrac{-4f(x) \pm 2\sqrt{3}f(x)}{2}$

$f'(x) = (-2 \pm \sqrt{3})f(x)$

Separating the variables:

$\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)} = -2 \pm \sqrt{3}$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$:

$\int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)} dx = \int (-2 \pm \sqrt{3}) dx$

$\ln |f(x)| = (-2 \pm \sqrt{3})x + C$

$f(x) = e^{(-2 \pm \sqrt{3})x + C}$

$f(x) = e^C \cdot e^{(-2 \pm \sqrt{3})x}$

Replacing $e^C$ with a new constant $c$:

$f(x) = c \cdot e^{(-2 \pm \sqrt{3})x}$

Answer: $c \cdot e^{(-2 \pm \sqrt{3})x}$

question.text: The solution of the differential equation $y^2 - x^2 \dfrac{dy}{dx} = xy \dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is ...

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $y^2 - x^2 \dfrac{dy}{dx} = xy \dfrac{dy}{dx}$

Rearranging the terms, we get:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y^2}{x^2 + xy}$

This is a homogeneous differential equation. Substitute $y = vx$, which gives $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = v + x \dfrac{dv}{dx}$

$v + x \dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{v^2 x^2}{x^2 + v x^2} = \dfrac{v^2}{1 + v}$

$x \dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{v^2}{1 + v} - v = \dfrac{v^2 - v - v^2}{1 + v} = \dfrac{-v}{1 + v}$

Separating the variables:

$\dfrac{1 + v}{v} dv = -\dfrac{dx}{x}$

$\left( \dfrac{1}{v} + 1 \right) dv = -\dfrac{dx}{x}$

Integrating both sides:

$\int \left( \dfrac{1}{v} + 1 \right) dv = -\int \dfrac{dx}{x}$

$\log|v| + v = -\log|x| + c$

Substituting $v = \dfrac{y}{x}$:

$\log\left|\dfrac{y}{x}\right| + \dfrac{y}{x} = -\log|x| + c$

$\log|y| - \log|x| + \dfrac{y}{x} = -\log|x| + c$

$\dfrac{y}{x} + \log|y| = c$

Answer: $\dfrac{y}{x} + \log|y| = c$

question.text: The solution of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x - y}{x + y}$, when $x = 0$ and $y = 0$ represents ....

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x - y}{x + y}$

Rearranging the terms, we get:

$(x + y)dy = (x - y)dx$

$x dy + y dy = x dx - y dx$

$x dy + y dx = x dx - y dy$

This can be written as exact differentials:

$d(xy) = x dx - y dy$

Integrating both sides, we get:

$\int d(xy) = \int x dx - \int y dy$

$xy = \dfrac{x^2}{2} - \dfrac{y^2}{2} + C$

$x^2 - 2xy - y^2 = -2C$

Given that $x = 0$ when $y = 0$, substituting these values gives:

$0^2 - 2(0)(0) - 0^2 = -2C \Rightarrow C = 0$

Substituting $C = 0$ back into the equation, we obtain:

$x^2 - 2xy - y^2 = 0$

This is a homogeneous equation of degree 2 in $x$ and $y$ (of the form $ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0$), which represents a pair of straight lines passing through the origin.

Answer: Pair of straight Lines

question.text: For the differential equation $(x^2 + y^2)\,dy = xy\,dx$, it is given that $y(1) = 1$ and $y(x_0) = e$, then the value of $x_0$ is _____

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $(x^2 + y^2)dy = xy dx$.

This can be rewritten as $\dfrac{dx}{dy} = \dfrac{x^2 + y^2}{xy} = \dfrac{x}{y} + \dfrac{y}{x}$.

Let $x = vy$, then $\dfrac{dx}{dy} = v + y\dfrac{dv}{dy}$.

Substituting this into the differential equation, we get:

$v + y\dfrac{dv}{dy} = v + \dfrac{1}{v}$

$y\dfrac{dv}{dy} = \dfrac{1}{v}$

$v dv = \dfrac{dy}{y}$

Integrating both sides, we get:

$\dfrac{v^2}{2} = \ln|y| + C$

Substituting $v = \dfrac{x}{y}$:

$\dfrac{x^2}{2y^2} = \ln|y| + C$

Given $y(1) = 1$, substituting $x = 1$ and $y = 1$:

$\dfrac{1}{2} = \ln(1) + C \Rightarrow C = \dfrac{1}{2}$

The particular solution is:

$\dfrac{x^2}{2y^2} = \ln|y| + \dfrac{1}{2}$

We are given $y(x_0) = e$, so substituting $x = x_0$ and $y = e$:

$\dfrac{x_0^2}{2e^2} = \ln(e) + \dfrac{1}{2}$

$\dfrac{x_0^2}{2e^2} = 1 + \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2}$

$x_0^2 = 3e^2$

$x_0 = \pm\sqrt{3}e$

Answer: $\pm\sqrt{3}\,e$

question.text: The equation of the curve passing through the point (0, 1) and having a slope of the tangent at point $P(x, y)$ is equal to $\dfrac{y}{x + y}$, is

solution.text:
Given the slope of the tangent is $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y}{x + y}$

Taking the reciprocal, we get:

$\dfrac{dx}{dy} = \dfrac{x + y}{y}$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{dx}{dy} - \dfrac{x}{y} = 1$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dx}{dy} + Px = Q$, where $P = -\dfrac{1}{y}$ and $Q = 1$.

Integrating Factor (IF) $= e^{\int -\dfrac{1}{y} dy} = e^{-\ln y} = \dfrac{1}{y}$

The solution is given by:

$x \cdot (\text{IF}) = \int Q \cdot (\text{IF}) dy + C$

$\Rightarrow x \left(\dfrac{1}{y}\right) = \int \dfrac{1}{y} dy + C$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{x}{y} = \ln y + C$

Since the curve passes through the point $(0, 1)$, substitute $x = 0$ and $y = 1$:

$\dfrac{0}{1} = \ln 1 + C \Rightarrow C = 0$

Therefore, the equation of the curve is:

$\dfrac{x}{y} = \ln y$

$\Rightarrow y = e^{\dfrac{x}{y}}$

Answer: $y = e^{\frac{x}{y}}$

question.text: The solution of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x+y}{x-y}$ is

options.label: A
options.text: $c(x^2 + y^2)^{\frac{1}{2}} + e^{\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{y^2}{x}\right)} = 0$, where c is an arbitrary constant

options.label: B
options.text: $c(x^2 + y^2)^{\frac{1}{2}} = e^{\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}$, where c is an arbitrary constant

options.label: C
options.text: $c(x^2 - y^2) = e^{\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}$, where c is an arbitrary constant

options.label: D
options.text: $c(x^2 + y^2) = e^{\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}$, where c is an arbitrary constant

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x+y}{x-y}$.

Substituting $y = vx$, we get $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$.

$v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{x+vx}{x-vx} = \dfrac{1+v}{1-v}$

$x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{1+v}{1-v} - v = \dfrac{1+v-v+v^2}{1-v} = \dfrac{1+v^2}{1-v}$

Separating the variables, we get:

$\dfrac{1-v}{1+v^2} dv = \dfrac{dx}{x}$

Integrating both sides:

$\int \dfrac{1}{1+v^2} dv - \int \dfrac{v}{1+v^2} dv = \int \dfrac{dx}{x}$

$\tan^{-1}v - \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(1+v^2) = \ln|x| + C$

Substituting $v = \dfrac{y}{x}$:

$\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(1+\dfrac{y^2}{x^2}\right) = \ln|x| + C$

$\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{x^2}\right) = \ln|x| + C$

$\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(x^2+y^2) + \ln|x| = \ln|x| + C$

$\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(x^2+y^2) = C$

$\ln(x^2+y^2)^{\dfrac{1}{2}} = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) - C$

$(x^2+y^2)^{\dfrac{1}{2}} = e^{\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) - C}$

$e^C (x^2+y^2)^{\dfrac{1}{2}} = e^{\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)}$

Letting $c = e^C$, we obtain:

$c(x^2+y^2)^{\dfrac{1}{2}} = e^{\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)}$

Answer: $c(x^2 + y^2)^{\frac{1}{2}} = e^{\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}$, where c is an arbitrary constant

question.text: The slope of the tangent at $(x, y)$ to the curve passing through $(2,1)$ is $\frac{x^2+y^2}{2 x y}$, then the equation of the curve is

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x^2+y^2}{2xy}$.

Rearranging the terms:

$2xy \, dy = (x^2+y^2) \, dx$

$2xy \, dy - y^2 \, dx = x^2 \, dx$

Dividing both sides by $x^2$:

$\dfrac{x(2y \, dy) - y^2 \, dx}{x^2} = dx$

$d\left(\dfrac{y^2}{x}\right) = dx$

Integrating both sides:

$\dfrac{y^2}{x} = x + C$

$y^2 = x^2 + Cx$

$x^2 - y^2 = -Cx$

Since the curve passes through $(2,1)$, substitute $x=2$ and $y=1$:

$2^2 - 1^2 = -C(2)$

$3 = -2C \Rightarrow -C = \dfrac{3}{2}$

Therefore, the equation of the curve is $x^2 - y^2 = \dfrac{3}{2}x$, which simplifies to $2(x^2 - y^2) = 3x$.

Answer: $2(x^2-y^2)=3x$

question.text: The general solution of differential equation $\left(y^2-x^2\right) \mathrm{d} x=x y$ dy $(x \neq 0)$ is

options.text: $2 x^2 \log x+\mathrm{y}^2+2 \mathrm{c} x^2=0$, where c is the constant of integration
$2 x^2 \log x-\mathrm{y}^2+2 \mathrm{c} x^2=0$, where c is the constant of integration
$x^2 \log x+\mathrm{y}^2+2 \mathrm{c} x^2=0$, where c is the constant of integration
$x^2 \log x-\mathrm{y}^2+2 \mathrm{c} x^2=0$, where c is the constant of integration

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $(y^2 - x^2) \mathrm{d}x = xy \mathrm{d}y$.

Rearranging the terms, we get:

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y^2 - x^2}{xy}$

This is a homogeneous differential equation. Substitute $y = vx$, which gives $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = v + x \dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}$.

Substituting these into the differential equation:

$v + x \dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{v^2 x^2 - x^2}{vx^2}$

$v + x \dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{v^2 - 1}{v}$

$x \dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{v^2 - 1}{v} - v$

$x \dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{v^2 - 1 - v^2}{v}$

$x \dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} = -\dfrac{1}{v}$

Separating the variables:

$v \mathrm{d}v = -\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{x}$

Integrating both sides:

$\int v \mathrm{d}v = -\int \dfrac{1}{x} \mathrm{d}x$

$\dfrac{v^2}{2} = -\log x - c$

Substituting back $v = \dfrac{y}{x}$:

$\dfrac{y^2}{2x^2} = -\log x - c$

Multiplying the entire equation by $2x^2$:

$y^2 = -2x^2 \log x - 2cx^2$

$2x^2 \log x + y^2 + 2cx^2 = 0$

Answer: $2 x^2 \log x+\mathrm{y}^2+2 \mathrm{c} x^2=0$, where c is the constant of integration

question.text: If $x \frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x}=\mathrm{y}(\log \mathrm{y}-\log x+1)$, then the solution of the equation is

options.text: $\log \frac{x}{\mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{cy}$, where c is the constant of integration
$\log \frac{\mathrm{y}}{x}=\mathrm{cy}$, where c is the constant of integration
$\log \frac{x}{\mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{c} x$, where c is the constant of integration
$\log \frac{\mathrm{y}}{x}=\mathrm{c} x$, where c is the constant of integration

solution.text:
The given differential equation is:

$x \dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x} = \mathrm{y}(\log \mathrm{y} - \log x + 1)$

Dividing both sides by $x$, we get:

$\dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x} = \dfrac{\mathrm{y}}{x} \left( \log \left( \dfrac{\mathrm{y}}{x} \right) + 1 \right)$

This is a homogeneous differential equation. Substitute $\mathrm{y} = v x$, which gives $\dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x} = v + x \dfrac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{d} x}$.

Substituting these into the equation:

$v + x \dfrac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{d} x} = v (\log v + 1)$

$v + x \dfrac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{d} x} = v \log v + v$

$x \dfrac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{d} x} = v \log v$

Separating the variables:

$\dfrac{\mathrm{dv}}{v \log v} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d} x}{x}$

Integrating both sides:

$\int \dfrac{1}{v \log v} \mathrm{dv} = \int \dfrac{1}{x} \mathrm{d} x$

$\log(\log v) = \log x + \log \mathrm{c}$

$\log(\log v) = \log(\mathrm{c} x)$

$\log v = \mathrm{c} x$

Substituting back $v = \dfrac{\mathrm{y}}{x}$:

$\log \left( \dfrac{\mathrm{y}}{x} \right) = \mathrm{c} x$

Answer: $\log \frac{\mathrm{y}}{x}=\mathrm{c} x$, where c is the constant of integration

question.text: If $x=\sec \theta-\cos \theta, y=\sec ^{10} \theta-\cos ^{10} \theta$ and $\left(x^2+4\right)\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{~d} x}\right)^2=\mathrm{k}\left(y^2+4\right)$, then the value of k is

solution.text:
Given $x = \sec \theta - \cos \theta$ and $y = \sec^{10} \theta - \cos^{10} \theta$.

Squaring and adding $4$ to both expressions:

$x^2 + 4 = (\sec \theta - \cos \theta)^2 + 4 = \sec^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta - 2 + 4 = \sec^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta + 2 = (\sec \theta + \cos \theta)^2$

$y^2 + 4 = (\sec^{10} \theta - \cos^{10} \theta)^2 + 4 = \sec^{20} \theta + \cos^{20} \theta - 2 + 4 = \sec^{20} \theta + \cos^{20} \theta + 2 = (\sec^{10} \theta + \cos^{10} \theta)^2$

Differentiating $x$ and $y$ with respect to $\theta$:

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = \sec \theta \tan \theta + \sin \theta = \tan \theta (\sec \theta + \cos \theta)$

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = 10 \sec^9 \theta (\sec \theta \tan \theta) - 10 \cos^9 \theta (-\sin \theta) = 10 \sec^{10} \theta \tan \theta + 10 \cos^9 \theta \sin \theta = 10 \tan \theta (\sec^{10} \theta + \cos^{10} \theta)$

Dividing the two derivatives to find $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$:

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}\theta}}{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}\theta}} = \dfrac{10 \tan \theta (\sec^{10} \theta + \cos^{10} \theta)}{\tan \theta (\sec \theta + \cos \theta)} = \dfrac{10 (\sec^{10} \theta + \cos^{10} \theta)}{\sec \theta + \cos \theta}$

Squaring both sides and multiplying by $x^2 + 4$:

$(x^2 + 4) \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\right)^2 = (\sec \theta + \cos \theta)^2 \times \dfrac{100 (\sec^{10} \theta + \cos^{10} \theta)^2}{(\sec \theta + \cos \theta)^2}$

$(x^2 + 4) \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\right)^2 = 100 (\sec^{10} \theta + \cos^{10} \theta)^2$

Substituting $y^2 + 4 = (\sec^{10} \theta + \cos^{10} \theta)^2$:

$(x^2 + 4) \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\right)^2 = 100 (y^2 + 4)$

Comparing this with the given equation $(x^2 + 4) \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\right)^2 = \mathrm{k}(y^2 + 4)$, we get $\mathrm{k} = 100$.

Answer: 100

question.text: The particular solution of the differential equation $(2 x-2 y+3) \mathrm{d} x-(x-y+1) \mathrm{d} y=0$ when $x=0, y=1$ is

solution.text:
Let $x-y+1=v$
$\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow 1-\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{~d} x}=\frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{~d} x} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{~d} x}=1-\frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{~d} x} \\
& \text { now } \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{~d} x}=\frac{2 x-2 y+3}{x-y+1} \\
& \Rightarrow 1-\frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{~d} x}=\frac{2 v+1}{v} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{~d} x}=1-\frac{2 v+1}{v}=\frac{-(v+1)}{v} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{v}{v+1} \mathrm{~d} v=-\mathrm{d} x \\
& \Rightarrow \int\left(1-\frac{1}{v+1}\right) \mathrm{d} v=-\int \mathrm{d} x \\
& \Rightarrow n-\log |n+1|=-x+c \\
& \Rightarrow(x-y+1)-\log (x-y+1+1)=-x+c \\
& \Rightarrow 2 x-y+1+\log (x-y+2)=c
\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} & \text { for } x=0, y=1 ; c=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 2 x-y-\log (x-y+2)+1=0\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{2 \sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{y}}=\log \left(c^{\prime} x \cdot \frac{y}{x}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow c \cdot e^{\frac{2 \sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{y}}}\end{aligned}$

question.text: The general solution of the differential equation $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{3 x+y}{x-y}$ is (where $C$ is a constant of integration.)

\therefore \frac{\mathrm{x}}{\mathrm{y}}+\log |\mathrm{x}|=\mathrm{c}
\end{array}$

question.text: General solution of the differential equation $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{x+y+1}{x+y-1}$ is given by

solution.text:
$\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{x+y+1}{x+y-1}$
Put $\quad x+y=t$
$\Rightarrow \quad 1+\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d t}{d x}$
$$
\begin{array}{lc}
\Rightarrow & \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d t}{d x}-1 \\
\therefore & \frac{d t}{d x}-1=\frac{t+1}{t-1} \\
\Rightarrow & \frac{d t}{d x}=\frac{t+1+t-1}{t-1} \\
\Rightarrow & \frac{d t}{d x}=\frac{2 t}{t-1} \\
\Rightarrow & \left(\frac{t-1}{2 t}\right) d t=d x \\
\Rightarrow & \left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2 t}\right) d t=d x
\end{array}
$$
On integrating, we get
$$
\frac{1}{2} t-\frac{1}{2} \log t=x+c_{1}
$$
$\begin{array}{lrl}\Rightarrow & t-\log t & =2 x+2 c_{1} \\ \Rightarrow & x+y-\log (x+y) & =2 x+2 c_{1} \\ \Rightarrow & y & =x+\log (x+y)+c\end{array}$

question.text: The solution of the differential equation $\left(3 x y+y^{2}\right) d x+\left(x^{2}+x y\right) d y=0$ is
The solution of the differential equation $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{x-y+3}{2(x-y)+5}$ is

solution.text:
Given differential equation is
$$
\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{x-y+3}{2(x-y)+5}
$$
Let $\quad x-y=v \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=1-\frac{d v}{d x}$
$\therefore$
$$
\frac{d v}{d x}=\frac{v+2}{2 v+5}
$$
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\Rightarrow \quad \int \frac{2 v+5}{v+2} d v=\int d x \\
\Rightarrow \quad \int\left(2+\frac{1}{v+2}\right) d v=\int d x
\end{array}
$$
$\Rightarrow \quad 2 v+\log (v+2)=x+c$
$\Rightarrow 2(x-y)+\log (x-y+2)=x+c$

question.text: Which of the following is not a correct pair of a linear differential equation and its integrating factor?

options.label: A
options.text: Linear differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y = 2x$, Integrating factor $= e^{-x}$

options.label: B
options.text: Linear differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = e^x$, Integrating factor $= e^x$

options.label: C
options.text: Linear differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = x + xy$, Integrating factor $= e^{\frac{x^2}{2}}$

options.label: D
options.text: Linear differential equation $x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y = x^2 \log x$, Integrating factor $= x^2$

solution.text:
A linear differential equation is of the form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$, and its integrating factor is given by $e^{\int P dx}$.

For the first option, the differential equation is $\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y = 2x$. Here $P = -1$.
Integrating factor $= e^{\int -1 dx} = e^{-x}$. This pair is correct.

For the second option, the differential equation is $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = e^x$. Here $P = 1$.
Integrating factor $= e^{\int 1 dx} = e^x$. This pair is correct.

For the third option, the differential equation is $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = x + xy \Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx} - xy = x$. Here $P = -x$.
Integrating factor $= e^{\int -x dx} = e^{-\dfrac{x^2}{2}}$. The given integrating factor is $e^{\dfrac{x^2}{2}}$, which is incorrect.

For the fourth option, the differential equation is $x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y = x^2 \log x \Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{2}{x}y = x \log x$. Here $P = \dfrac{2}{x}$.
Integrating factor $= e^{\int \dfrac{2}{x} dx} = e^{2\log x} = x^2$. This pair is correct.

Thus, the incorrect pair is the third option.

Answer: Linear differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = x + xy$, Integrating factor $= e^{\frac{x^2}{2}}$

question.text: The general solution of the differential equation $(x + 1)\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y = e^x(x + 1)^2$ is given by:

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $(x + 1)\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y = e^x(x + 1)^2$

Dividing the entire equation by $(x + 1)$, we get:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} - \dfrac{1}{x + 1}y = e^x(x + 1)$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)$, where $P(x) = -\dfrac{1}{x + 1}$ and $Q(x) = e^x(x + 1)$.

The integrating factor (IF) is given by:

$\text{IF} = e^{\int P(x) dx} = e^{\int -\dfrac{1}{x + 1} dx} = e^{-\ln(x + 1)} = \dfrac{1}{x + 1}$

The general solution is:

$y \cdot (\text{IF}) = \int Q(x) \cdot (\text{IF}) dx + c$

$y \cdot \dfrac{1}{x + 1} = \int e^x(x + 1) \cdot \dfrac{1}{x + 1} dx + c$

$\dfrac{y}{x + 1} = \int e^x dx + c$

$\dfrac{y}{x + 1} = e^x + c$

$y = (x + 1)(e^x + c)$

Answer: $y = (x + 1)(e^x + c)$

question.text: If the curve $y = f(x)$ passes through the point $(1, 2)$ and satisfies the differential equation $x dy + (y + x^3 y^2)dx = 0$, then the equation of curve is...

solution.text:
The given differential equation is:

$x dy + (y + x^3 y^2)dx = 0$

Rearranging the terms, we get:

$x dy + y dx = -x^3 y^2 dx$

Using the product rule of differentiation, $d(xy) = x dy + y dx$. Substituting this into the equation:

$d(xy) = -x^3 y^2 dx$

Dividing both sides by $(xy)^2$:

$\dfrac{d(xy)}{(xy)^2} = -x dx$

Integrating both sides:

$\int \dfrac{d(xy)}{(xy)^2} = -\int x dx$

$-\dfrac{1}{xy} = -\dfrac{x^2}{2} + C$

Since the curve passes through the point $(1, 2)$, we substitute $x = 1$ and $y = 2$ into the equation:

$-\dfrac{1}{1 \times 2} = -\dfrac{1^2}{2} + C$

$-\dfrac{1}{2} = -\dfrac{1}{2} + C \Rightarrow C = 0$

Substituting $C = 0$ back into the integrated equation:

$-\dfrac{1}{xy} = -\dfrac{x^2}{2}$

$\dfrac{1}{xy} = \dfrac{x^2}{2}$

$x^3 y = 2$

Answer: $x^3 y = 2$

question.text: If $g(x)$ denotes the integrating factor of the differential equation $x \log x \dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = 2 \log x$ and $\int g(x) \, dx = h(x)[g(x) - 1] + c$, then $h(x) = $.........

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $x \log x \dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = 2 \log x$.

Dividing the entire equation by $x \log x$, we get:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{1}{x \log x} y = \dfrac{2}{x}$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + P y = Q$, where $P = \dfrac{1}{x \log x}$.

The integrating factor $g(x)$ is given by:

$g(x) = e^{\int P \, dx} = e^{\int \dfrac{1}{x \log x} \, dx}$

Let $\log x = t$, then $\dfrac{1}{x} dx = dt$.

$\int \dfrac{1}{x \log x} \, dx = \int \dfrac{1}{t} \, dt = \log t = \log(\log x)$

Therefore, $g(x) = e^{\log(\log x)} = \log x$.

Now, we evaluate $\int g(x) \, dx$:

$\int g(x) \, dx = \int \log x \, dx$

Using integration by parts:

$\int \log x \cdot 1 \, dx = x \log x - \int x \cdot \dfrac{1}{x} \, dx = x \log x - x + c = x(\log x - 1) + c$

We are given that $\int g(x) \, dx = h(x)[g(x) - 1] + c$.

Substituting $g(x) = \log x$, we get:

$x(\log x - 1) + c = h(x)[\log x - 1] + c$

Comparing both sides, we obtain:

$h(x) = x$

Answer: $x$

question.text: If $yf(x)=g(x)+c$ where $c$ is an arbitrary constant such that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+yg(x)=f(x)$ and $[f(x)]^2-[g(x)]^2=1$, then $\int f(x)\cdot g(x)\,dx=$ ...

solution.text:
Given the differential equation:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y g(x) = f(x)$

The solution is given as:

$y f(x) = g(x) + c$

Differentiating the solution with respect to $x$, we get:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} f(x) + y f'(x) = g'(x)$

Substitute $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = f(x) - y g(x)$ from the given differential equation into the differentiated equation:

$(f(x) - y g(x)) f(x) + y f'(x) = g'(x)$

$f(x)^2 - y f(x) g(x) + y f'(x) = g'(x)$

$y (f'(x) - f(x) g(x)) + f(x)^2 - g'(x) = 0$

Since this equation must hold true for any arbitrary constant $c$, it must be an identity in $y$. Therefore, the coefficient of $y$ and the remaining terms must independently be zero:

$f'(x) - f(x) g(x) = 0 \Rightarrow f'(x) = f(x) g(x)$

$f(x)^2 - g'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow g'(x) = f(x)^2$

We can verify this is consistent with the given relation $[f(x)]^2 - [g(x)]^2 = 1$. Differentiating it gives $2f(x)f'(x) - 2g(x)g'(x) = 0$, which holds true upon substituting $f'(x)$ and $g'(x)$.

We need to evaluate the integral $\int f(x) g(x) \,dx$. Using the relation $f'(x) = f(x) g(x)$, we get:

$\int f(x) g(x) \,dx = \int f'(x) \,dx = f(x) + c$

Answer: $f(x)+c$

question.text: The general solution of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{y}{x} = x^2 + 5$ is ....

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{1}{x}y = x^2 + 5$.

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$, where $P = \dfrac{1}{x}$ and $Q = x^2 + 5$.

The integrating factor is $e^{\int P dx} = e^{\int \dfrac{1}{x} dx} = e^{\ln x} = x$.

Multiplying the equation by the integrating factor, the solution is given by:

$y \cdot x = \int x(x^2 + 5) dx + C$

$xy = \int (x^3 + 5x) dx + C$

$xy = \dfrac{x^4}{4} + \dfrac{5x^2}{2} + C$

Rearranging the terms, we get:

$\dfrac{x^4}{4} + \dfrac{5x^2}{2} - xy = -C$

Taking $-C = c$, the general solution is:

$\dfrac{x^4}{4} + \dfrac{5x^2}{2} - xy = c$

Answer: $\dfrac{x^4}{4} + \dfrac{5x^2}{2} - xy = c$

question.text: If $\tan x$ is an integrating factor of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$, then $P$ can be

solution.text:
The integrating factor of the linear differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$ is given by $e^{\int P dx}$.

Given that the integrating factor is $\tan x$, we have:

$e^{\int P dx} = \tan x$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:

$\int P dx = \ln(\tan x)$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$:

$P = \dfrac{d}{dx} (\ln(\tan x))$

$P = \dfrac{1}{\tan x} \cdot \sec^2 x$

$P = \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x}$

$P = \dfrac{1}{\sin x \cos x}$

$P = \dfrac{2}{2 \sin x \cos x}$

$P = \dfrac{2}{\sin 2x}$

$P = 2 \csc 2x$

Answer: $2\csc 2x$

question.text: If the solution of the differential equation $(1 + x^3)\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 6x^2y = 1 + x^2$ is $y = \dfrac{1}{(1 + x^3)^s}\left[x + \dfrac{x^p}{p} + \dfrac{x^q}{q} + \dfrac{x^r}{r} + c\right]$, then the LCM of $p, q, r$ and $s$ is...

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $(1 + x^3)\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 6x^2y = 1 + x^2$.

Dividing by $(1 + x^3)$, we get a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)$:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{6x^2}{1 + x^3}y = \dfrac{1 + x^2}{1 + x^3}$

The integrating factor (IF) is given by:

$\text{IF} = e^{\int P(x) dx} = e^{\int \dfrac{6x^2}{1 + x^3} dx}$

Let $1 + x^3 = t$, then $3x^2 dx = dt$, which gives $6x^2 dx = 2 dt$.

$\int \dfrac{6x^2}{1 + x^3} dx = \int \dfrac{2}{t} dt = 2 \ln t = \ln(t^2) = \ln((1 + x^3)^2)$

Thus, $\text{IF} = e^{\ln((1 + x^3)^2)} = (1 + x^3)^2$.

Multiplying the differential equation by the IF, we get:

$\dfrac{d}{dx} \left[ y (1 + x^3)^2 \right] = \dfrac{1 + x^2}{1 + x^3} \times (1 + x^3)^2$

$\dfrac{d}{dx} \left[ y (1 + x^3)^2 \right] = (1 + x^2)(1 + x^3)$

$\dfrac{d}{dx} \left[ y (1 + x^3)^2 \right] = 1 + x^2 + x^3 + x^5$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$:

$y (1 + x^3)^2 = \int (1 + x^2 + x^3 + x^5) dx$

$y (1 + x^3)^2 = x + \dfrac{x^3}{3} + \dfrac{x^4}{4} + \dfrac{x^6}{6} + c$

$y = \dfrac{1}{(1 + x^3)^2} \left[ x + \dfrac{x^3}{3} + \dfrac{x^4}{4} + \dfrac{x^6}{6} + c \right]$

Comparing this with the given solution $y = \dfrac{1}{(1 + x^3)^s}\left[x + \dfrac{x^p}{p} + \dfrac{x^q}{q} + \dfrac{x^r}{r} + c\right]$, we find:

$s = 2$

The set of values for $\{p, q, r\}$ is $\{3, 4, 6\}$.

We need to find the LCM of $p, q, r$ and $s$, which is the LCM of $3, 4, 6,$ and $2$.

$\text{LCM}(2, 3, 4, 6) = 12$

Answer: $12$

question.text: The integrating factor of the differential equation $x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y = x^2 \log x$ is

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y = x^2 \log x$.

Dividing the entire equation by $x$, we get:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{2}{x}y = x \log x$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$, where $P = \dfrac{2}{x}$ and $Q = x \log x$.

The integrating factor (IF) is given by $e^{\int P dx}$.

$\text{IF} = e^{\int \dfrac{2}{x} dx}$

$\text{IF} = e^{2 \log x}$

$\text{IF} = e^{\log x^2}$

$\text{IF} = x^2$

Answer: $x^2$

question.text: The general solution of the differential equation $x\sin x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + (x\cos x + \sin x)y = \sin x$ is

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $x\sin x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + (x\cos x + \sin x)y = \sin x$

Observing the left hand side, it can be rewritten using the product rule of differentiation:

$x\sin x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin x) = \sin x$

$\dfrac{d}{dx}(xy\sin x) = \sin x$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$:

$\int \dfrac{d}{dx}(xy\sin x) dx = \int \sin x dx$

$xy\sin x = -\cos x + c$

$xy\sin x + \cos x = c$

Answer: $xy\sin x + \cos x = c$

question.text: The general solution of the differential equation $\sec y + (x - e^{\sin y})\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$ is...

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $\sec y + (x - e^{\sin y})\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$

Rearranging the terms, we get:

$\sec y \dfrac{dx}{dy} + x - e^{\sin y} = 0$

$\dfrac{dx}{dy} + x \cos y = e^{\sin y} \cos y$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dx}{dy} + P(y)x = Q(y)$, where $P(y) = \cos y$ and $Q(y) = e^{\sin y} \cos y$.

The integrating factor (IF) is:

$IF = e^{\int \cos y dy} = e^{\sin y}$

Multiplying the equation by the integrating factor and integrating, the solution is given by:

$x \cdot IF = \int Q(y) \cdot IF dy + c$

$x e^{\sin y} = \int e^{\sin y} \cos y \cdot e^{\sin y} dy + c$

$x e^{\sin y} = \int e^{2\sin y} \cos y dy + c$

Let $\sin y = t$, then $\cos y dy = dt$. The integral becomes:

$\int e^{2t} dt = \dfrac{e^{2t}}{2} = \dfrac{e^{2\sin y}}{2}$

Thus, the general solution is:

$x e^{\sin y} = \dfrac{e^{2\sin y}}{2} + c$

Answer: $xe^{\sin y} = \dfrac{e^{2\sin y}}{2} + c$

question.text: If $y = e^{-mx}$ is a solution of the differential equation $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} + 4\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 3y = 0$, then the values of $m$ are

solution.text:
Given $y = e^{-mx}$

Differentiating with respect to $x$, we get:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -m e^{-mx}$

$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = m^2 e^{-mx}$

Substituting these into the given differential equation $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} + 4\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 3y = 0$:

$m^2 e^{-mx} + 4(-m e^{-mx}) + 3(e^{-mx}) = 0$

$e^{-mx}(m^2 - 4m + 3) = 0$

Since $e^{-mx} \neq 0$ for any finite $x$, we have:

$m^2 - 4m + 3 = 0$

$(m - 1)(m - 3) = 0$

$m = 1, 3$

Answer: $1, 3$

question.text: The integrating factor of the differential equation $(1 + t^2) + \left(x - e^{\tan^{-1}t}\right)\dfrac{dt}{dx} = 0$ is

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $(1 + t^2) + \left(x - e^{\tan^{-1}t}\right)\dfrac{dt}{dx} = 0$

Rearranging the terms, we get:

$(1 + t^2)\dfrac{dx}{dt} + x - e^{\tan^{-1}t} = 0$

$\dfrac{dx}{dt} + \dfrac{1}{1 + t^2}x = \dfrac{e^{\tan^{-1}t}}{1 + t^2}$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dx}{dt} + Px = Q$, where $P = \dfrac{1}{1 + t^2}$ and $Q = \dfrac{e^{\tan^{-1}t}}{1 + t^2}$

The integrating factor is given by $e^{\int P dt}$

$IF = e^{\int \dfrac{1}{1 + t^2} dt} = e^{\tan^{-1}t}$

Answer: $e^{\tan^{-1}t}$

question.text: The solution of the differential equation $\left(x + 2y^3\right)\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y = 0$ is

options.label: A
options.text: $x = (c + y^2)y$, where c is the constant of integration

options.label: B
options.text: $y = (c + y^2)x$, where c is the constant of integration

options.label: C
options.text: $x = (c + y)y$, where c is the constant of integration

options.label: D
options.text: $y = (c + x^2)$, where c is the constant of integration

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $(x + 2y^3)\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y = 0$

Rearranging the terms, we get:

$\dfrac{dx}{dy} = \dfrac{x + 2y^3}{y}$

$\dfrac{dx}{dy} - \dfrac{1}{y}x = 2y^2$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dx}{dy} + P(y)x = Q(y)$, where $P(y) = -\dfrac{1}{y}$ and $Q(y) = 2y^2$.

The integrating factor (IF) is:

$IF = e^{\int -\dfrac{1}{y} dy} = e^{-\ln y} = \dfrac{1}{y}$

Multiplying the differential equation by the integrating factor and integrating, the solution is given by:

$x \cdot (IF) = \int Q(y) \cdot (IF) dy + c$

$x \left(\dfrac{1}{y}\right) = \int 2y^2 \left(\dfrac{1}{y}\right) dy + c$

$\dfrac{x}{y} = \int 2y dy + c$

$\dfrac{x}{y} = y^2 + c$

$x = y(y^2 + c)$

Answer: $x = (c + y^2)y$, where c is the constant of integration

question.text: The solution of the differential equation $x^2 \dfrac{dy}{dx} - xy = 1$ is...

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $x^2 \dfrac{dy}{dx} - xy = 1$

Dividing by $x^2$, we get:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} - \dfrac{1}{x}y = \dfrac{1}{x^2}$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$, where $P = -\dfrac{1}{x}$ and $Q = \dfrac{1}{x^2}$

Integrating Factor (IF) = $e^{\int P dx} = e^{\int -\dfrac{1}{x} dx} = e^{-\ln x} = \dfrac{1}{x}$

The solution is given by:

$y \cdot (\text{IF}) = \int Q \cdot (\text{IF}) dx + c$

$y \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) = \int \dfrac{1}{x^2} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) dx + c$

$\dfrac{y}{x} = \int x^{-3} dx + c$

$\dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{x^{-2}}{-2} + c$

$\dfrac{y}{x} = -\dfrac{1}{2x^2} + c$

Multiplying the entire equation by $2x^2$, we get:

$2xy = -1 + 2cx^2$

$2xy - 2cx^2 + 1 = 0$

Answer: $2xy - 2cx^2 + 1 = 0$

question.text: The general solution of the differential equation $(x+y)\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1$ is

options.label: A
options.text: $x + y + 1 = c$, where $c$ is a constant of integration

options.label: B
options.text: $x + y + 1 = ce^y$, where $c$ is a constant of integration

options.label: C
options.text: $x + y + 1 = ce^{-y}$, where $c$ is a constant of integration

options.label: D
options.text: $x + y - 1 = ce^{-y}$, where $c$ is a constant of integration

solution.text:
Given differential equation is $(x+y)\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1$

Rewriting the equation, we get $\dfrac{dx}{dy} = x + y$

$\dfrac{dx}{dy} - x = y$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dx}{dy} + Px = Q$, where $P = -1$ and $Q = y$.

Integrating Factor (IF) $= e^{\int P dy} = e^{\int -1 dy} = e^{-y}$

The general solution is given by $x \cdot (\text{IF}) = \int Q \cdot (\text{IF}) dy + c$

$x e^{-y} = \int y e^{-y} dy + c$

Using integration by parts,

$x e^{-y} = y(-e^{-y}) - \int 1 \cdot (-e^{-y}) dy + c$

$x e^{-y} = -y e^{-y} - e^{-y} + c$

Multiplying both sides by $e^y$, we get

$x = -y - 1 + c e^y$

$x + y + 1 = c e^y$

Answer: $x + y + 1 = ce^y$, where $c$ is a constant of integration

question.text: The solution of the differential equation $2x\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y = 3$ represents a family of

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $2x\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y = 3$

Rearranging the terms, we get:

$2x\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y + 3$

Separating the variables:

$\dfrac{dy}{y + 3} = \dfrac{dx}{2x}$

Integrating both sides:

$\int \dfrac{dy}{y + 3} = \int \dfrac{dx}{2x}$

$\ln(y + 3) = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln x + \ln c$

$\ln(y + 3) = \ln(c\sqrt{x})$

$y + 3 = c\sqrt{x}$

Squaring both sides, we get:

$(y + 3)^2 = c^2 x$

This is an equation of the form $Y^2 = 4aX$, which represents a family of parabolas.

Answer: parabola

question.text: The solution of the differential equation $x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = x^3 y^6$, is...

solution.text:
The given differential equation is:

$x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = x^3 y^6$

Dividing the entire equation by $x y^6$:

$\dfrac{1}{y^6} \dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{1}{x y^5} = x^2$

Let $v = \dfrac{1}{y^5} = y^{-5}$.

Differentiating with respect to $x$:

$\dfrac{dv}{dx} = -5 y^{-6} \dfrac{dy}{dx} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{y^6} \dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{1}{5} \dfrac{dv}{dx}$

Substituting this into the differential equation:

$-\dfrac{1}{5} \dfrac{dv}{dx} + \dfrac{1}{x} v = x^2$

$\dfrac{dv}{dx} - \dfrac{5}{x} v = -5 x^2$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dv}{dx} + P v = Q$, where $P = -\dfrac{5}{x}$ and $Q = -5 x^2$.

The Integrating Factor (IF) is:

$IF = e^{\int -\dfrac{5}{x} dx} = e^{-5 \ln x} = x^{-5}$

The solution is given by:

$v \cdot x^{-5} = \int (-5 x^2) \cdot x^{-5} dx + c$

$v x^{-5} = \int -5 x^{-3} dx + c$

$v x^{-5} = -5 \left( \dfrac{x^{-2}}{-2} \right) + c$

$v x^{-5} = \dfrac{5}{2} x^{-2} + c$

Multiplying both sides by $x^5$:

$v = \dfrac{5}{2} x^3 + c x^5$

Substituting back $v = \dfrac{1}{y^5}$:

$\dfrac{1}{y^5} = \dfrac{5}{2} x^3 + c x^5$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{y^5} = \dfrac{5}{2}x^3 + cx^5$

question.text: The integrating factor of the differential equation $x \frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x}+\mathrm{y} \log x=x \mathrm{e}^x \cdot x^{\frac{-1}{2}} \log x(x>0)$ is

solution.text:
The given differential equation is:

$x \dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x} + y \log x = x \mathrm{e}^x \cdot x^{\dfrac{-1}{2}} \log x$

Dividing the entire equation by $x$, we get:

$\dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x} + \left(\dfrac{\log x}{x}\right) y = \mathrm{e}^x \cdot x^{\dfrac{-1}{2}} \log x$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x} + P y = Q$, where $P = \dfrac{\log x}{x}$.

The integrating factor (I.F.) is given by $\mathrm{e}^{\int P \mathrm{d} x}$.

$\int P \mathrm{d} x = \int \dfrac{\log x}{x} \mathrm{d} x$

Let $\log x = t \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{x} \mathrm{d} x = \mathrm{d} t$.

$\int t \mathrm{d} t = \dfrac{t^2}{2} = \dfrac{(\log x)^2}{2}$

Therefore, the integrating factor is:

$\text{I.F.} = \mathrm{e}^{\dfrac{(\log x)^2}{2}} = \mathrm{e}^{\dfrac{1}{2} (\log x) (\log x)}$

Using the property $\mathrm{e}^{a \log x} = x^a$, we can write:

$\text{I.F.} = (\mathrm{e}^{\log x})^{\dfrac{1}{2} \log x} = x^{\dfrac{1}{2} \log x} = (x^{\dfrac{1}{2}})^{\log x} = (\sqrt{x})^{\log x}$

Answer: $(\sqrt{x})^{\log x}$

question.text: The solution of the differential equation. $(1+x) \frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x}-x \mathrm{y}=1-x$ is

options.text: $\mathrm{y}(1+x)=x+\mathrm{ce}^x$, where c is the constant of integration
$\mathrm{y}(1+x)=\mathrm{ce}^x$, where c is the constant of integration
$\mathrm{y}(1-x)=x-\mathrm{ce}^x$, where c is the constant of integration
$\mathrm{y}(1+x)=x~ \mathrm{ce}^{-x}$, where c is the constant of integration

solution.text:
The given differential equation is:

$(1+x) \dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x} - x \mathrm{y} = 1-x$

Dividing the entire equation by $(1+x)$, we get:

$\dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x} - \left(\dfrac{x}{1+x}\right) \mathrm{y} = \dfrac{1-x}{1+x}$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x} + P\mathrm{y} = Q$, where $P = -\dfrac{x}{1+x}$ and $Q = \dfrac{1-x}{1+x}$.

The integrating factor (IF) is given by:

$\text{IF} = e^{\int P \mathrm{d} x} = e^{-\int \dfrac{x}{1+x} \mathrm{d} x}$

$\int -\dfrac{x}{1+x} \mathrm{d} x = -\int \dfrac{x+1-1}{1+x} \mathrm{d} x = -\int \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{1+x}\right) \mathrm{d} x = -x + \ln(1+x)$

$\text{IF} = e^{-x + \ln(1+x)} = e^{-x} \cdot e^{\ln(1+x)} = (1+x)e^{-x}$

The general solution is given by:

$\mathrm{y} \cdot \text{IF} = \int Q \cdot \text{IF} \mathrm{d} x + \mathrm{c}$

$\mathrm{y}(1+x)e^{-x} = \int \left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right) (1+x)e^{-x} \mathrm{d} x + \mathrm{c}$

$\mathrm{y}(1+x)e^{-x} = \int (1-x)e^{-x} \mathrm{d} x + \mathrm{c}$

Using integration by parts on the right side:

$\int (1-x)e^{-x} \mathrm{d} x = (1-x)\int e^{-x} \mathrm{d} x - \int \left( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x}(1-x) \int e^{-x} \mathrm{d} x \right) \mathrm{d} x$

$= (1-x)(-e^{-x}) - \int (-1)(-e^{-x}) \mathrm{d} x$

$= (x-1)e^{-x} - \int e^{-x} \mathrm{d} x$

$= (x-1)e^{-x} - (-e^{-x})$

$= x e^{-x} - e^{-x} + e^{-x} = x e^{-x}$

Substituting this back into the equation:

$\mathrm{y}(1+x)e^{-x} = x e^{-x} + \mathrm{c}$

Multiplying both sides by $e^x$, we get:

$\mathrm{y}(1+x) = x + \mathrm{c}e^x$

Answer: $\mathrm{y}(1+x)=x+\mathrm{ce}^x$, where c is the constant of integration

question.text: The integrating factor of $\mathrm{y}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x}(x \mathrm{y})=x(\sin x+\log x)$ is

solution.text:
The given differential equation is:

$\mathrm{y} + \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x}(x \mathrm{y}) = x(\sin x + \log x)$

Expanding the derivative term, we get:

$\mathrm{y} + \mathrm{y} + x \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathrm{y}}{\mathrm{d} x} = x(\sin x + \log x)$

$x \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathrm{y}}{\mathrm{d} x} + 2\mathrm{y} = x(\sin x + \log x)$

Dividing the entire equation by $x$, we obtain:

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathrm{y}}{\mathrm{d} x} + \dfrac{2}{x} \mathrm{y} = \sin x + \log x$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathrm{y}}{\mathrm{d} x} + P\mathrm{y} = Q$, where $P = \dfrac{2}{x}$.

The integrating factor (I.F.) is given by:

$\text{I.F.} = e^{\int P \mathrm{d}x}$

$\text{I.F.} = e^{\int \dfrac{2}{x} \mathrm{d}x}$

$\text{I.F.} = e^{2 \log x}$

$\text{I.F.} = e^{\log x^2} = x^2$

Answer: $x^2$

question.text: If $\mathrm{y}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x}(x \mathrm{y})=x(\sin x+\log x)$ then

options.text:
$\mathrm{y}=\cos x+\frac{2 \sin x}{x}+\frac{2}{x^2} \cos x+\frac{x}{3} \log x-\frac{x}{9}+\frac{\mathrm{c}}{x^2}$,
where $c$ is the constant of integration.

$\mathrm{y}=-\cos x-\frac{2}{x} \sin x+\frac{2}{x^2} \cos x+\frac{x}{3} \log x-\frac{x}{9}+\frac{\mathrm{c}}{x^2}$
where $c$ is the constant of integration.

$\mathrm{y}=-\cos x+\frac{2}{x} \sin x+\frac{2}{x^2} \cos x+\frac{x}{3} \log x-\frac{x}{9}+\frac{\mathrm{c}}{x^2}$,
where c is the constant of integration.

$\mathrm{y}=\cos x-\frac{2}{x} \sin x+\frac{2}{x^3} \cos x+\frac{x}{3} \log x-\frac{x}{9}+\frac{\mathrm{c}}{x^2}$,
where c is the constant of integration.

solution.text:
The given differential equation is:

$y + \dfrac{d}{dx}(xy) = x(\sin x + \log x)$

Expanding the derivative using the product rule:

$y + x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = x(\sin x + \log x)$

$x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y = x(\sin x + \log x)$

Dividing the entire equation by $x$:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{2}{x}y = \sin x + \log x$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$, where $P = \dfrac{2}{x}$ and $Q = \sin x + \log x$.

The integrating factor (IF) is:

$IF = e^{\int P dx} = e^{\int \dfrac{2}{x} dx} = e^{2\log x} = x^2$

Multiplying the differential equation by the integrating factor:

$x^2 \dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2xy = x^2(\sin x + \log x)$

$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2 y) = x^2 \sin x + x^2 \log x$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$:

$x^2 y = \int x^2 \sin x dx + \int x^2 \log x dx + c$

Using integration by parts for the first integral:

$\int x^2 \sin x dx = x^2(-\cos x) - \int 2x(-\cos x) dx$

$= -x^2 \cos x + 2 \int x \cos x dx$

$= -x^2 \cos x + 2\left(x \sin x - \int \sin x dx\right)$

$= -x^2 \cos x + 2x \sin x + 2\cos x$

Using integration by parts for the second integral:

$\int x^2 \log x dx = (\log x)\left(\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right) - \int \dfrac{1}{x} \left(\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right) dx$

$= \dfrac{x^3}{3} \log x - \int \dfrac{x^2}{3} dx$

$= \dfrac{x^3}{3} \log x - \dfrac{x^3}{9}$

Substituting the integrals back into the equation:

$x^2 y = -x^2 \cos x + 2x \sin x + 2\cos x + \dfrac{x^3}{3} \log x - \dfrac{x^3}{9} + c$

Dividing by $x^2$:

$y = -\cos x + \dfrac{2}{x} \sin x + \dfrac{2}{x^2} \cos x + \dfrac{x}{3} \log x - \dfrac{x}{9} + \dfrac{c}{x^2}$

Answer: $\mathrm{y}=-\cos x+\frac{2}{x} \sin x+\frac{2}{x^2} \cos x+\frac{x}{3} \log x-\frac{x}{9}+\frac{\mathrm{c}}{x^2}$, where c is the constant of integration.

question.text: The equation of the curve passing through the origin and satisfying the equation $\left(1+x^2\right) \frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x}+2 x y=4 x^2$, is

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $\left(1+x^2\right) \dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x}+2 x y=4 x^2$.

Notice that the left hand side is the exact derivative of $y(1+x^2)$ with respect to $x$.

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x} \left[ y(1+x^2) \right] = 4x^2$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we get:

$y(1+x^2) = \int 4x^2 \, \mathrm{d}x$

$y(1+x^2) = \dfrac{4x^3}{3} + C$

Since the curve passes through the origin $(0,0)$, we substitute $x = 0$ and $y = 0$ into the equation:

$0(1+0^2) = \dfrac{4(0)^3}{3} + C$

$C = 0$

Substituting $C = 0$ back into the equation, we get:

$y(1+x^2) = \dfrac{4x^3}{3}$

$3y(1+x^2) = 4x^3$

Answer: $3\left(1+x^2\right) \mathrm{y}=4 x^3$

question.text: The solution of $\left(1+y^2\right)+\left(x-\mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y}\right) \frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x}=0$ is

options.text: $2 x \mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y}=\mathrm{e}^{2 \tan ^{-1} y}+\mathrm{k}$, where k is the constant of integration
$x \cdot \mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} \mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} \mathrm{y}}+\mathrm{k}$, where k is the constant of integration
$x \cdot \mathrm{e}^{2 \tan ^{-1} \mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} \mathrm{y}}+\mathrm{k}$, where k is the constant of integration
$x=2+\mathrm{k} \cdot \mathrm{e}^{-\tan ^{-1} \mathrm{y}} \quad$, where k is the constant of integration

solution.text:
The given differential equation is:

$\left(1+y^2\right)+\left(x-\mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y}\right) \dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x}=0$

Rearranging the terms, we get:

$\left(x-\mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y}\right) \dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x} = -\left(1+y^2\right)$

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y} = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y} - x}{1+y^2}$

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y} + \dfrac{1}{1+y^2} x = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y}}{1+y^2}$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y} + P(y)x = Q(y)$, where $P(y) = \dfrac{1}{1+y^2}$ and $Q(y) = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y}}{1+y^2}$.

The integrating factor (IF) is:

$\text{IF} = \mathrm{e}^{\int P(y) \mathrm{d}y} = \mathrm{e}^{\int \dfrac{1}{1+y^2} \mathrm{d}y} = \mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y}$

The general solution is given by:

$x \cdot (\text{IF}) = \int Q(y) \cdot (\text{IF}) \mathrm{d}y + \mathrm{C}$

$x \cdot \mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y} = \int \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y}}{1+y^2} \cdot \mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y} \mathrm{d}y + \mathrm{C}$

$x \cdot \mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y} = \int \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{2 \tan ^{-1} y}}{1+y^2} \mathrm{d}y + \mathrm{C}$

Let $t = \tan ^{-1} y$, then $\mathrm{d}t = \dfrac{1}{1+y^2} \mathrm{d}y$. The integral becomes:

$\int \mathrm{e}^{2t} \mathrm{d}t = \dfrac{1}{2} \mathrm{e}^{2t} = \dfrac{1}{2} \mathrm{e}^{2 \tan ^{-1} y}$

Substituting this back into the solution:

$x \cdot \mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y} = \dfrac{1}{2} \mathrm{e}^{2 \tan ^{-1} y} + \mathrm{C}$

Multiplying the entire equation by $2$:

$2x \mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y} = \mathrm{e}^{2 \tan ^{-1} y} + 2\mathrm{C}$

Let $2\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{k}$, where $\mathrm{k}$ is the constant of integration:

$2x \mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y} = \mathrm{e}^{2 \tan ^{-1} y} + \mathrm{k}$

Answer: $2 x \mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} y}=\mathrm{e}^{2 \tan ^{-1} y}+\mathrm{k}$, where k is the constant of integration

question.text:
The general solution of
$x(x-1) \frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x}=x^3(2 x-1)+(x-2) \mathrm{y}$ is

options.text: $y(x-1)=x^3+c(x-1)$, where $c$ is the constant of integration.
$\mathrm{y}=x^3(x-1)+\mathrm{c}, \quad$ where c is the constant of integration.
$y(x-1)=x^3(x-1)+c x^2$, where $c$ is the constant of integration.
$y(x-1)=x^3(x-1)+c, \quad$ where $c$ is the constant of integration.

solution.text:
The given differential equation is:

$x(x-1) \dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x} - (x-2) \mathrm{y} = x^3(2 x-1)$

Dividing the entire equation by $x(x-1)$, we get:

$\dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x} - \dfrac{x-2}{x(x-1)} \mathrm{y} = \dfrac{x^2(2 x-1)}{x-1}$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x} + P \mathrm{y} = Q$, where:

$P = -\dfrac{x-2}{x(x-1)}$ and $Q = \dfrac{x^2(2 x-1)}{x-1}$

Using partial fractions for $P$:

$\dfrac{x-2}{x(x-1)} = \dfrac{2}{x} - \dfrac{1}{x-1}$

$\Rightarrow P = \dfrac{1}{x-1} - \dfrac{2}{x}$

The integrating factor (IF) is:

$\text{IF} = e^{\int P \mathrm{d} x} = e^{\int \left(\dfrac{1}{x-1} - \dfrac{2}{x}\right) \mathrm{d} x}$

$\text{IF} = e^{\ln(x-1) - 2\ln x} = e^{\ln\left(\dfrac{x-1}{x^2}\right)} = \dfrac{x-1}{x^2}$

The general solution is given by:

$y \cdot \text{IF} = \int Q \cdot \text{IF} \mathrm{d} x + c$

$y \left(\dfrac{x-1}{x^2}\right) = \int \dfrac{x^2(2 x-1)}{x-1} \cdot \dfrac{x-1}{x^2} \mathrm{d} x + c$

$y \left(\dfrac{x-1}{x^2}\right) = \int (2 x-1) \mathrm{d} x + c$

$y \left(\dfrac{x-1}{x^2}\right) = x^2 - x + c$

$y \left(\dfrac{x-1}{x^2}\right) = x(x-1) + c$

Multiplying both sides by $x^2$, we get:

$y(x-1) = x^3(x-1) + c x^2$

Answer: $y(x-1)=x^3(x-1)+c x^2$, where $c$ is the constant of integration.

question.text: The general solution of the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{~d} x}=y \tan x-y^2 \sec x$ is

options.text: $\tan x=(\mathrm{c}+\sec x) y$, where c is constant of integration.
$\sec y=(\mathrm{c}+\tan y) x$, where c is constant of integration.
$\sec x=(\mathrm{c}+\tan x) y$, where c is constant of integration.
$\cos y=(\mathrm{c}+\tan y)$, where c is constant of integration.

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $\dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} - y \tan x = -y^2 \sec x$

Dividing the entire equation by $y^2$, we get:

$\dfrac{1}{y^2} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} - \dfrac{1}{y} \tan x = -\sec x$

Let $\dfrac{1}{y} = t$, then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives $-\dfrac{1}{y^2} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d} t}{\mathrm{d} x}$

Substituting this into the equation, we get:

$-\dfrac{\mathrm{d} t}{\mathrm{d} x} - t \tan x = -\sec x$

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d} t}{\mathrm{d} x} + t \tan x = \sec x$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{\mathrm{d} t}{\mathrm{d} x} + P t = Q$, where $P = \tan x$ and $Q = \sec x$.

Integrating Factor (IF) $= e^{\int P \mathrm{d} x} = e^{\int \tan x \mathrm{d} x} = e^{\ln(\sec x)} = \sec x$

The general solution is given by:

$t \times \text{IF} = \int (Q \times \text{IF}) \mathrm{d} x + \mathrm{c}$

$t \sec x = \int \sec x \cdot \sec x \mathrm{d} x + \mathrm{c}$

$t \sec x = \int \sec^2 x \mathrm{d} x + \mathrm{c}$

$t \sec x = \tan x + \mathrm{c}$

Substituting back $t = \dfrac{1}{y}$, we get:

$\dfrac{1}{y} \sec x = \tan x + \mathrm{c}$

$\sec x = (\mathrm{c} + \tan x) y$

Answer: $\sec x=(\mathrm{c}+\tan x) y$, where c is constant of integration.

question.text: The differential equation of $y=\mathrm{e}^x\left(\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b} x+x^2\right)$ is

solution.text:
The given equation is $y = \mathrm{e}^x(a + bx + x^2)$

Multiplying both sides by $\mathrm{e}^{-x}$:

$y \mathrm{e}^{-x} = a + bx + x^2$

Differentiating with respect to $x$:

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} \mathrm{e}^{-x} - y \mathrm{e}^{-x} = b + 2x$

$\left( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} - y \right) \mathrm{e}^{-x} = b + 2x$

Differentiating again with respect to $x$:

$\left( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} - \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} \right) \mathrm{e}^{-x} - \left( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} - y \right) \mathrm{e}^{-x} = 2$

$\left( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} - 2\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} + y \right) \mathrm{e}^{-x} = 2$

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} - 2\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} + y = 2\mathrm{e}^x$

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} - 2\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} - 2\mathrm{e}^x + y = 0$

Answer: $\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 y}{\mathrm{~d} x^2}-2 \frac{\mathrm{~d} y}{\mathrm{~d} x}-2 \mathrm{e}^x+y=0$

question.text:
Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $x \frac{\mathrm{~d} y}{\mathrm{~d} x}+y=x \log x,(x\gt1)$
If $2(y(2))=\log 4-1$ then the value of $y(\mathrm{e})$ is

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $x \dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} + y = x \log x$.

This can be rewritten as:

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x} (x y) = x \log x$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we get:

$x y = \int x \log x \mathrm{d} x + C$

Using integration by parts:

$x y = \log x \int x \mathrm{d} x - \int \left( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x} (\log x) \int x \mathrm{d} x \right) \mathrm{d} x$

$x y = \dfrac{x^2}{2} \log x - \int \dfrac{1}{x} \left( \dfrac{x^2}{2} \right) \mathrm{d} x$

$x y = \dfrac{x^2}{2} \log x - \dfrac{x^2}{4} + C$

We are given that $2 y(2) = \log 4 - 1$. Substituting $x = 2$ into the equation:

$2 y(2) = \dfrac{2^2}{2} \log 2 - \dfrac{2^2}{4} + C$

$2 y(2) = 2 \log 2 - 1 + C$

$2 y(2) = \log 4 - 1 + C$

Since $2 y(2) = \log 4 - 1$, we have $C = 0$.

The particular solution is:

$x y = \dfrac{x^2}{2} \log x - \dfrac{x^2}{4}$

To find $y(\mathrm{e})$, substitute $x = \mathrm{e}$:

$\mathrm{e} y(\mathrm{e}) = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^2}{2} \log \mathrm{e} - \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^2}{4}$

Since $\log \mathrm{e} = 1$:

$\mathrm{e} y(\mathrm{e}) = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^2}{2} - \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^2}{4} = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^2}{4}$

$y(\mathrm{e}) = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}}{4}$

Answer: $\frac{\mathrm{e}}{4}$

question.text: If $\cos x \dfrac{\mathrm{~d} y}{\mathrm{~d} x}-y \sin x=6 x, 0 \lt x \lt \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, then general solution of the differential equation is

options.text: $y=\cos x+3 x^2+\mathrm{c}$, where c is a constant of integration.
$y+\cos x=3 x^2+\mathrm{c}$, where c is a constant of integration.
$y=3 x^2 \cos x+\cos x$, where c is a constant of integration.
$y \cdot \cos x=3 x^2+\mathrm{c}$, where c is a constant of integration.

solution.text:
Given differential equation is $\cos x \dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} - y \sin x = 6 x$

This can be written as $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x}(y \cos x) = 6 x$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we get

$\int \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x}(y \cos x) \mathrm{d} x = \int 6 x \mathrm{d} x$

$y \cdot \cos x = 3 x^2 + \mathrm{c}$

where $\mathrm{c}$ is a constant of integration.

Answer: $y \cdot \cos x=3 x^2+\mathrm{c}$, where c is a constant of integration.

question.text: Integrating factor of the differential equation $\dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{~d} x}+y=\dfrac{1+y}{x}$ is

solution.text:
The given differential equation is:

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} + y = \dfrac{1+y}{x}$

Rearranging the terms, we get:

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} + y - \dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{1}{x}$

$\dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} + \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{x}\right)y = \dfrac{1}{x}$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} + P y = Q$, where $P = 1 - \dfrac{1}{x}$ and $Q = \dfrac{1}{x}$.

The integrating factor (I.F.) is given by $\mathrm{e}^{\int P \mathrm{d} x}$.

$\text{I.F.} = \mathrm{e}^{\int \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{x}\right) \mathrm{d} x}$

$\text{I.F.} = \mathrm{e}^{x - \ln x}$

$\text{I.F.} = \mathrm{e}^x \cdot \mathrm{e}^{-\ln x}$

$\text{I.F.} = \mathrm{e}^x \cdot \dfrac{1}{x} = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^x}{x}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mathrm{e}^x}{x}$

question.text: The curve satisfying the differential equation $y \mathrm{~d} x-\left(x+3 y^2\right) \mathrm{dy}=0$ and passing through the point $(1,1)$ also passes through the point

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $y \mathrm{d}x - (x + 3y^2) \mathrm{dy} = 0$

Rearranging the terms, we get $y \mathrm{d}x - x \mathrm{dy} = 3y^2 \mathrm{dy}$

Dividing both sides by $y^2$, we get $\dfrac{y \mathrm{d}x - x \mathrm{dy}}{y^2} = 3 \mathrm{dy}$

This can be written as $\mathrm{d}\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) = 3 \mathrm{dy}$

Integrating both sides, we get $\dfrac{x}{y} = 3y + C$

Since the curve passes through $(1, 1)$, substituting $x = 1$ and $y = 1$ gives $1 = 3 + C \Rightarrow C = -2$

The equation of the curve is $x = 3y^2 - 2y$

Checking the given options, for $y = \dfrac{1}{3}$, we get $x = 3\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 - 2\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{2}{3} = -\dfrac{1}{3}$

Thus, the curve passes through $\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{1}{3}\right)$.

Answer: $\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{1}{3}\right)$

question.text: If $y=y(x)$ is the solution of the differential equation $x \dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x}+2 y=x^2$ satisfying $y(1)=1$, then the value of $y\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $x \dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x}+2 y=x^2$

Dividing by $x$, we get $\dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x}+\dfrac{2}{x} y=x$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{d} x} + P y = Q$. The integrating factor is $IF = e^{\int \dfrac{2}{x} \mathrm{d} x} = e^{2 \ln x} = x^2$

Multiplying the equation by the integrating factor, we get $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x}(y x^2) = x^3$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we get $y x^2 = \dfrac{x^4}{4} + C$

Given $y(1)=1$, substituting $x=1$ and $y=1$ gives $1 = \dfrac{1}{4} + C \Rightarrow C = \dfrac{3}{4}$

The solution to the differential equation is $y x^2 = \dfrac{x^4}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4}$

Substituting $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$, we get $y\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{64} + \dfrac{3}{4}$

$y\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{49}{64}$

$y\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{49}{16}$

Answer: $\dfrac{49}{16}$

question.text:
Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\sin x \dfrac{\mathrm{~d} y}{\mathrm{~d} x}+y \cos x=4 x, x \in(0, \pi)$.
If $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=0$, then $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ is equal to

solution.text:
The given differential equation is $\sin x \dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} + y \cos x = 4x$.

This can be rewritten as $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x} (y \sin x) = 4x$.

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we get:

$\int \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x} (y \sin x) \mathrm{d} x = \int 4x \, \mathrm{d} x$

$y \sin x = 2x^2 + C$

Given $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0$, substituting $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $y = 0$:

$0 \cdot \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)^2 + C$

$0 = \dfrac{\pi^2}{2} + C \Rightarrow C = -\dfrac{\pi^2}{2}$

Thus, the solution is $y \sin x = 2x^2 - \dfrac{\pi^2}{2}$.

To find $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$, substitute $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$:

$y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)^2 - \dfrac{\pi^2}{2}$

$y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = 2\left(\dfrac{\pi^2}{36}\right) - \dfrac{\pi^2}{2}$

$y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\pi^2}{18} - \dfrac{\pi^2}{2}$

$y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\pi^2 - 9\pi^2}{18} = -\dfrac{8\pi^2}{18} = -\dfrac{4\pi^2}{9}$

$y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{8}{9}\pi^2$

Answer: $-\dfrac{8}{9} \pi^2$
